cards.meaning: the day before today
cards.example: Yesterday I walked to the old bridge by the river.
cards.note: Say 'last night', not 'yesterday night'.

cards.meaning: before now; it comes after a length of time
cards.example: I moved to this street three weeks ago.
cards.note: Put ago after the time: 'ten minutes ago', not 'ago ten minutes'.

cards.meaning: the one just before this one
cards.example: Last week I visited my cousin in the next town.
cards.note: No 'the' before it here: 'last Monday', not 'the last Monday'.

cards.meaning: to get to a place at the end of a trip
cards.example: Our bus arrived at six in the evening.
cards.note: Arrive at a building or place, arrive in a town or country. Never 'arrive to'.

cards.meaning: to go away from a place
cards.example: I left home at eight and caught the early train.
cards.note: Irregular: leave, left.

cards.meaning: the travelling from one place to another
cards.example: The journey to the coast took three hours.

cards.meaning: to change the direction you are going
cards.example: Turn left at the traffic lights.

cards.meaning: in one line, without turning
cards.example: Go straight on for about two minutes.

cards.meaning: the place where two streets meet
cards.example: There is a small café on the corner.

cards.meaning: a picture that shows roads and places
cards.example: Can you show me the station on the map?

cards.meaning: every time
cards.example: I always drink a glass of water in the morning.
cards.note: Put it before the main verb, but after be: 'I always walk', 'I am always early'.

cards.meaning: most times, but not every time
cards.example: I usually take the bus, but today I walked.

cards.meaning: many times
cards.example: We often eat outside when it is warm.

cards.meaning: some of the time, not always
cards.example: I sometimes feel nervous before a phone call.

cards.meaning: not at any time
cards.example: My neighbour never forgets my birthday.
cards.note: Never already means 'not': say 'I never eat meat', not 'I don't never eat meat'.

cards.meaning: a word we use when we compare two things
cards.example: The bus is slower than the train.
cards.note: Don't confuse it with 'then', which is about time.

cards.meaning: better than all the others
cards.example: This is the best bakery in the town.
cards.note: good, better, the best.

cards.meaning: having a lot to do; or full of people and traffic
cards.example: I'm busy on Monday, but I'm free on Tuesday.
cards.note: busy, busier, the busiest.

cards.meaning: a little afraid that something bad may happen
cards.example: I was worried about the move, but it went well.
cards.note: Say 'worried about something'.

cards.meaning: very happy about something good that is coming
cards.example: The children are excited about the trip.

cards.meaning: a bit afraid before something new or important
cards.example: I was nervous before the meeting, and that is normal.

cards.meaning: something you have decided to do
cards.example: What are your plans for the weekend?
cards.note: As a verb: 'plan to do something'.

cards.meaning: not busy; with nothing planned
cards.example: Are you free on Friday evening?
cards.note: Free can also mean 'costs nothing'.

cards.text: Excuse me, how do I get to …?
cards.meaning: a polite way to ask for directions
cards.example: Excuse me, how do I get to the post office?

cards.meaning: keep walking or driving in the same direction
cards.example: Go straight on past the church.

cards.meaning: you will see it on your right-hand side
cards.example: Walk to the end of the street. The library is on your right.
cards.note: Always 'on' your left or right.

cards.text: Sorry, could you say that again?
cards.meaning: a polite way to ask someone to repeat something
cards.example: Sorry, could you say that again? Left or right at the corner?
cards.note: Everyone asks this. It is a normal part of any conversation.

cards.meaning: a friendly question about someone's last weekend
cards.example: Hi Tom! How was your weekend?
cards.note: Answer with 'It was …': 'It was great, thanks.'

cards.meaning: a question that asks about someone's past activities
cards.example: You went to the coast? What did you do there?
goes_with: What did you do at the weekend?

cards.meaning: a way to ask the other person the same question
cards.example: I'm from Manchester. What about you?
cards.note: It keeps a conversation going in both directions.

cards.meaning: one time every week
cards.example: I go swimming once a week, on Saturday mornings.
cards.note: These phrases usually go at the end of the sentence.

cards.meaning: a question to check if someone has time
cards.example: Are you free on Saturday afternoon?
goes_with: Do you have any plans for …?

cards.meaning: yes, happily: a warm way to accept an invitation
cards.example: Dinner on Friday? I'd love to. Thank you!
cards.note: I'd = I would.

cards.meaning: a polite way to say no to an invitation
cards.example: Sorry, I can't. I'm going to work late on Friday.
cards.note: Add a short reason if you like.

cards.meaning: goodbye until the time we agreed
cards.example: Seven o'clock at the café? Great, see you then.

cards.meaning: a way to thank someone who asked you to come
cards.example: Thanks for inviting me. I had a lovely evening.

cards.meaning: say what you did at a finished time
cards.example: Last summer, I went to the mountains.
cards.note: Use a past verb in the second blank.

cards.meaning: say how long before now something happened
cards.example: I moved here two years ago.

cards.meaning: a yes or no question about the past
cards.example: Did you sleep well?
cards.note: After did, use the base verb: 'Did you go?', not 'Did you went?'

cards.meaning: a past question that starts with who, what, where, when, why or how
cards.example: Where did you stay?

cards.meaning: say what you normally do on a certain day
cards.example: I usually visit my mum on Sundays.

cards.meaning: compare two things
cards.example: The river path is quieter than the main road.
cards.note: With long adjectives, use more: 'more beautiful than'.

cards.meaning: say that one thing is top of a group
cards.example: This is the oldest house in the village.
cards.note: With long adjectives, use the most: 'the most beautiful'.

cards.meaning: say what you have decided to do in the future
cards.example: I'm going to visit my sister next month.

cards.meaning: a polite way to invite someone
cards.example: Would you like to come for dinner on Friday?

lessons.title: Where I Was Yesterday
lessons.why: Most small talk is about what happened: your weekend, your trip, your day.
lessons.rule: Use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time: yesterday, last week, two days ago. Regular verbs add -ed (walk, walked), but many common verbs are irregular (go, went; leave, left; take, took). In questions and negatives, use did or didn't with the base verb: Did you arrive? I didn't stop.

passage.title: The road to the crossroads
passage.text:
Two days ago, I left my small town early in the morning. I took a bus to the city, and then I walked to the station. The journey was long, but it wasn't boring. On the train, I talked to an old man with a green hat. He told me about the crossroads, the place where four roads meet.

I arrived at the crossroads late that night. It was dark and I was very tired. I didn't know the way to the guest house, so I asked a woman in a shop. She was kind, and she walked with me to the door.

Yesterday, I got up late. I had breakfast in a small café and I watched the people. Some went north to the mountains. Some went south to the sea. A man with a big bag sat down next to me and asked, 'Did you arrive this morning?' I said, 'No, two days ago.'

Last year, I didn't travel at all. This year, I want to see everything.

drills.sentence: We ___ at the station two hours ago.
drills.hint: Look at the time words at the end of the sentence.
drills.why: 'Two hours ago' is a finished time, so we use the past simple: arrive becomes arrived.

options: I goed to the market yesterday.
I went to the market yesterday.
I go to the market yesterday.
drills.hint: Go is one of the irregular verbs.
drills.why: Go is irregular: the past is went, not goed. 'Yesterday' tells us we need the past.

drills.sentence: Did you left early this morning?
drills.answer: Did you leave early this morning?
drills.hint: Look at the verb that comes after did.
drills.why: After did, use the base verb. Did already shows that it is the past.

drills.answer: I didn't take the bus last week.
drills.hint: Start with the person and put the time at the end.
drills.why: A past negative is person + didn't + base verb. Time words like 'last week' often go at the end.

drills.sentence: She ___ the house at seven and caught the early bus.
drills.hint: The second verb, caught, is in the past. The first one should match.
drills.why: Leave is irregular: leave, left. Both actions are finished, so both verbs are past.

answers: The train was late, so we arrived after midnight.
The train was late so we arrived after midnight.
We arrived after midnight because the train was late.
drills.hint: One thing happened because of the other.
drills.why: So introduces a result; because introduces a reason.

drills.prompt: In the passage, when did the writer arrive at the crossroads?
drills.hint: Look at what the writer tells the man in the café.
drills.why: The writer left home two days ago and arrived late that same night, so the answer to the man is 'two days ago'.

write.prompt: Write about a journey you made. Where did you go, how did you travel and what happened on the way? Use at least four past verbs.

speak.prompt: Tell the Guide about your day yesterday: where you went, what you did and who you saw. There is no hurry; pause whenever you like.

lessons.check: What did you do last weekend? Answer in two sentences with past verbs.

lessons.title: Which Way to the Station?
lessons.why: Asking for and giving directions lets you move around a new place and help the people you meet.

passage.title: Two visitors at the crossroads
passage.text:
A visitor stopped me at the crossroads this morning. She had a map in her hand, but she looked confused.

'Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?' she asked.

'Go straight on along this road,' I said. 'At the second corner, turn left. Walk past the bank, and the station is on your right.'

'Sorry, could you say that again, please?'

'Of course. Straight on, then left at the second corner. The station is on your right, opposite the bank.'

She followed the road on her map with her finger. 'Straight on, second corner, left. Thank you!'

Ten minutes later, a man asked me the way to the library. The library is not easy to find, because it is behind the market. This time, I drew a small map for him on a piece of paper. He looked at it, smiled and turned right at the first corner. Directions are easier with a picture.

drills.prompt: You are lost and want the bus station. What do you say to a stranger?
options: Excuse me, how do I get to the bus station?
drills.hint: Look for the polite start.
drills.why: 'Excuse me' politely gets someone's attention, and 'How do I get to …?' is the usual question for directions.

drills.sentence: Turn left at the ___, and the café is on your right.
drills.hint: Where do two streets meet?
drills.why: A corner is where two streets meet, so it is a place where you can turn.

drills.answer: Go straight on and turn right at the bank.
drills.hint: It starts with a verb, like an instruction.
drills.why: Directions use the base verb as an instruction: go, turn, walk.

drills.sentence: The museum is in your left.
drills.answer: The museum is on your left.
drills.hint: Check the small word before 'your left'.
drills.why: We say on your left and on your right.

drills.prompt: You didn't catch all the directions. What can you say?
options: Sorry, could you say that again?
Sorry, can you go straight on?
Sorry, is it on the map yesterday?
drills.hint: You want to hear the same words one more time.
drills.why: 'Could you say that again?' asks someone to repeat. It is a normal, polite question that people ask all the time.

answers: When you see the river, turn right.
Turn right when you see the river.
drills.hint: Which small word tells us the moment something happens?
drills.why: When joins two actions and shows the moment for the second one.

drills.prompt: In the passage, why did the writer draw a map for the man?
options: Because the library is hard to find
Because the man had no money
drills.hint: Read the part about the library again.
drills.why: The library is behind the market and not easy to find, so a small map helped.

write.prompt: A friend is coming to your home for the first time. Write directions from the nearest bus stop or station to your door.

speak.prompt: Ask the Neighbour how to get to a place near your home, like a shop or a park. If you miss a step, ask them to say it again.

lessons.check: How do you get from your home to the nearest shop? Give two or three steps.

lessons.title: Questions for the Neighbour
lessons.why: Good questions show interest in people, and they let the other person do some of the talking.
lessons.rule: A direct wh- question starts with a question word: who, what, where, when, why or how. In the past, use question word + did + person + base verb: Where did you go? With be, put was or were before the person: Where were you? How was your weekend?

passage.title: Meeting Rosa
passage.text:
On my third day, I met my neighbour, Rosa, outside our building. She is friendly, and she likes questions.

'Hello! How was your weekend?' she asked.

'It was good, thanks. I went to the market by the river.'

'Oh, lovely. What did you buy?'

'Some bread and a blue cup. What about you? What did you do?'

'I visited my brother. He lives in the hills. Why did you come to the crossroads?'

'I wanted a change. At first I was nervous, because I didn't know anyone. Now I'm excited about my new job.'

'When did you start?'

'On Monday. Where did you live before this street?'

'In a small flat near the station. It was very noisy! Were you worried about the move?'

'A little. But not now.'

Rosa smiled. 'Good. Who did you meet this week?'

'Just you, and the woman in the shop.'

'Then come to the café on Friday. I can introduce you to everyone.'

drills.sentence: Where ___ you go on holiday last year?
drills.hint: 'Last year' is the past, and 'go' is a base verb.
drills.why: A past wh- question is question word + did + person + base verb.

drills.answer: What time did you arrive last night?
drills.hint: Start with the two question words.
drills.why: What time + did + person + base verb, with the time at the end.

drills.hint: After did, check the form of the verb.
drills.why: Did already shows the past, so the main verb stays in the base form: go, not went.

drills.prompt: Your neighbour says, 'I went to the coast.' Which question asks for the reason?
drills.hint: Which question word asks for a reason?
drills.why: Why asks for a reason, when asks for a time, and how asks about the way.

drills.sentence: ___ was the film? It was really funny.
drills.hint: The answer describes what the film was like.
drills.why: How was …? asks for someone's opinion or feeling about something.

drills.prompt: You answered your neighbour's question. How can you ask the same question back?
drills.hint: It is three words and ends with 'you'.
drills.why: 'What about you?' turns the same question back to the other person and keeps the conversation going.

answers: I was nervous because it was my first day.
It was my first day, so I was nervous.
It was my first day so I was nervous.
drills.hint: Which part is the reason?
drills.why: Because introduces the reason; so introduces the result.

write.prompt: Write six questions you would like to ask a new neighbour. Use at least four different question words, and make two of them about the past.

speak.prompt: Meet the Neighbour. Answer their questions about your weekend, then ask them at least three wh- questions back.

lessons.check: Ask one question about the past with 'where' and one with 'why'.

lessons.title: How Often?
lessons.why: Frequency words let you describe your life and habits, which is one of the first things people ask about.
lessons.rule: Adverbs of frequency say how often: always, usually, often, sometimes, never. Put them before the main verb (I usually walk) but after am, is or are (I am always early). Phrases like once a week or twice a month usually go at the end.

passage.title: Life at the crossroads
passage.text:
Rosa is a baker. She always gets up at five o'clock, even on Sundays. She usually opens the bakery at seven, and there is often a queue outside the door. People love her bread.

I am never up at five! I usually get up at half past seven. I sometimes buy a roll from Rosa on my way to work. Once a week, on Friday, I buy a big cake for my colleagues.

In the evening, Rosa is often tired, but she is never bored. She sometimes plays cards with the old men at the café on the corner. I usually cook at home, and I often call my sister. We talk about our week. Sometimes I feel nervous before a phone call, and that's fine. My sister is always patient, and we never hurry. We usually talk for an hour.

drills.sentence: I ___ drink coffee. I don't like it at all.
drills.hint: The person doesn't like coffee.
drills.why: Never means not at any time, which matches 'I don't like it at all'.

drills.hint: Where does the frequency word go when the verb is 'is'?
drills.why: With be, the frequency word comes after the verb: is always, am never, are often.

drills.answer: We usually have dinner at seven.
drills.hint: The frequency word comes before the main verb.
drills.why: Frequency words usually go between the person and the main verb.

drills.prompt: Which sentence means 'most days, but not every day'?
drills.hint: Always is every day and never is no days.
drills.why: Usually means most times, but not every time.

drills.sentence: I go swimming once a ___, every Saturday morning.
drills.hint: How often does Saturday come?
drills.why: Saturday comes once every week, so 'once a week' fits.

answers: I sometimes feel tired, but I always finish my work.
I sometimes feel tired but I always finish my work.
drills.hint: The second idea is a surprise after the first.
drills.why: But joins two ideas that contrast.

drills.prompt: In the passage, how often does the writer buy a cake?
drills.hint: Look for the day of the week.
drills.why: The writer buys a big cake once a week, on Friday.

write.prompt: Describe a normal week in your life. Use always, usually, often, sometimes and never at least once each.

speak.prompt: Speak alone: say five sentences about your week, one with each frequency word. Pause between them as long as you like.

lessons.check: How often do you cook? Answer with a frequency word in the right place.

lessons.title: Two Roads to the Sea
lessons.why: Comparing helps you make choices and explain them, and understanding comparisons helps you follow advice.
lessons.rule: To compare two things, add -er to short adjectives and use than: cheaper than, bigger than. With longer adjectives, use more: more beautiful than. To say one thing is top of a group, use the + -est or the most: the cheapest, the most beautiful. Some are irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst.

passage.title: Which road to the sea?
passage.text:
From the crossroads, two roads go to the sea. The guide explained them to me.

'The north road is shorter than the south road,' she said. 'It takes two hours by car. But it is busier, especially on Saturdays, and it isn't very pretty.'

'And the south road?'

'The south road is longer. The journey takes three and a half hours. But it is quieter and much more beautiful. It goes through the hills and past three small lakes. The biggest lake has a café next to it. They make the best fish soup in the country!'

'Which way is the cheapest?'

'The train. It costs eight pounds, and the bus costs twelve. But the train only goes on the north side.'

In the end, I chose the south road. I wasn't in a hurry, and I wanted to see the lakes. It was the most beautiful journey of my year.

drills.prompt: In the passage, which road is shorter?
drills.hint: Look at the first thing the guide says.
drills.why: The guide says the north road is shorter than the south road: two hours, not three and a half.

drills.prompt: According to the passage, what is the cheapest way to the sea?
drills.hint: Compare the two prices in the passage.
drills.why: The train costs eight pounds and the bus costs twelve, so the train is the cheapest.

drills.sentence: The south road is ___ than the north road.
drills.hint: We are comparing two roads, and the sentence has 'than'.
drills.why: With two things and than, use the -er form: quieter than.

drills.sentence: My flat is more big than yours.
drills.answer: My flat is bigger than yours.
drills.hint: Big is a short adjective.
drills.why: Short adjectives take -er, not more. Big doubles the g: bigger.

drills.sentence: This is the ___ café in town. The coffee is wonderful.
drills.hint: It is top of all the cafés in town, and 'the' comes before it.
drills.why: Good is irregular: good, better, the best. Use the best for the top of a group.

drills.answer: It was the most beautiful journey of my year.
drills.hint: Long adjectives do not take -est. What comes before them instead?
drills.why: For the top of a group with a long adjective, use the most + adjective + noun.

parts: The south road is more beautiful.
answers: The north road is faster, but the south road is more beautiful.
The north road is faster but the south road is more beautiful.
drills.hint: Each road has a different good point.
drills.why: But joins two ideas that contrast.

write.prompt: Compare two places you know, such as two towns, shops or parks. Which one do you prefer, and why? Use at least one -er word and one 'the most' or '-est' word.

speak.prompt: Ask the Guide to help you choose between two places to visit. Compare them together, then decide.

lessons.check: What is the best place in your town, and why is it better than another place?

lessons.title: An Invitation Next Door
lessons.why: Inviting people and talking about plans is how neighbours become friends.
lessons.rule: Use am, is or are + going to + base verb for plans you have already decided: I'm going to visit my cousin next week. For a question, put am, is or are first: Are you going to come? To invite someone, say Would you like to …? and answer with I'd love to or Sorry, I can't.

passage.title: Messages under the door
passage.text:
Hi Rosa,
I hope you're well. Are you free on Saturday evening? I'm going to have a small dinner at my flat to say thank you to my neighbours. You helped me a lot when I arrived.
Would you like to come? I'm going to make soup and fresh bread (not as good as yours!). Tom from the second floor is going to bring some music. We're going to start at seven, but come later if you're busy.
Please let me know by Thursday.
Sam

The next morning, Sam found two replies under the door.

Hi Sam,
What a kind idea! I'd love to come. My brother is visiting, but he's going to leave on Saturday morning, so I have no plans in the evening. I'm going to bring a cake.
See you then,
Rosa

Hi Sam,
Thank you for asking. Sorry, I can't come. I'm going to work late on Saturday. Have a lovely evening!
Ana (top floor)

drills.sentence: Next month, I'm going ___ visit my grandparents.
drills.hint: Which small word always follows 'going' in a plan?
drills.why: The plan form is going to + base verb.

drills.sentence: We going to watch a film tonight.
drills.answer: We're going to watch a film tonight.
accept: We are going to watch a film tonight.
drills.hint: Something small is missing before 'going'.
drills.why: Going to needs am, is or are: I'm, you're, we're, she's going to.

drills.answer: Are you going to come to the party?
drills.hint: It is a question, so it starts with a form of be.
drills.why: In a going to question, am, is or are comes before the person.

drills.prompt: Your neighbour invites you, but you are busy. What do you say?
options: Sorry, I can't. I'm going to work late.
I'd love to. I'm going to work late.
drills.hint: You need to say no politely and give a reason.
drills.why: 'Sorry, I can't' says no politely, and a short reason makes it friendly.

options: Would you like to come for a walk on Sunday?
Did you go for a walk on Sunday?
drills.hint: An invitation asks someone to join you.
drills.why: Would you like to …? is a polite way to invite someone.

drills.sentence: Thanks for the invitation! I'd ___ to come.
drills.hint: After I'd (I would), use the base verb.
drills.why: I'd love to is would + base verb, a warm way to say yes.

parts: We're going to have the picnic next week.
answers: It's going to rain tomorrow, so we're going to have the picnic next week.
It's going to rain tomorrow so we're going to have the picnic next week.
We're going to have the picnic next week because it's going to rain tomorrow.
drills.hint: The rain is the reason for the change.
drills.why: So introduces the result; because introduces the reason.

drills.prompt: In the passage, why can Rosa come on Saturday evening?
options: Her brother is going to leave in the morning.
She is going to work late.
Tom is going to bring music.
drills.hint: Read Rosa's reply again.
drills.why: Rosa's brother is going to leave on Saturday morning, so she has no plans in the evening.

write.prompt: Write a short message inviting a neighbour or friend to something. Say what it is, when and where, and ask them to reply.

speak.prompt: Invite the Neighbour to something you are going to do this weekend. Agree on a day and a time together.

lessons.check: What are you going to do next weekend? Invite someone to join you.

placement.sentence: I ___ to the cinema last night.
This bag is ___ than that one.
